WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Bush signed an executive order Friday expanding U.S. sanctions against Zimbabwe, the White House said. About 200 victims of election violence seek safety outside the U.S. Embassy in Harare, Zimbabwe, this month. "The new executive order significantly enhances our ability to designate individuals in and entities connected to the Mugabe regime," Bush said in a written statement that calls the Zimbabwean government under president Robert Mugabe "illegitimate." Just after the announcement, the Treasury Department said it has designated for sanctions 17 entities, including three government-owned or controlled companies used by Mugabe and his government "to illegally siphon revenue and foreign exchange from the Zimbabwean people," as well as one individual. "This action is a direct result of the Mugabe regime's continued politically motivated violence, disregarding calls from the Southern African Development Community, the African Union and the United Nations to halt the attacks," the White House said. "The regime has also continued its ban against NGO activities that would provide assistance to the suffering and vulnerable people of Zimbabwe. No regime should ignore the will of its own people and calls from the international community without consequences." The U.S. has been pushing for sanctions against Zimbabwe since Mugabe ignored a U.N. Security Council appeal to postpone a presidential runoff election June 27. The vote initially was intended to be a runoff between Mugabe and opposition candidate Morgan Tsvangirai, who did not win the presidency outright in the general election, according to government tallies. But Tsvangirai, of the Movement for Democratic Change, withdrew just before the vote, saying Mugabe's supporters had orchestrated a campaign of beatings, intimidation and murders against Tsvangirai supporters. Earlier this month, Russia and China vetoed a Security Council resolution pushed by the United States, Britain and France that would have imposed international sanctions on Mugabe and senior members of his government. Bush said last week he was "displeased" at the vetoes, but the Treasury and State Departments were working on potential U.S. action. Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Jendayi Frazer told members of Congress last week that more than 100 people have been murdered, more than 3,000 have been injured by beatings or torture and more than 30,000 have been driven from their homes because of violence that broke out after the general election. Entities designated by the Treasury Department include Minerals Marketing Corp. of Zimbabwe, the company that serves as the sole marketing and export agent for all minerals mined in Zimbabwe except gold and silver; Zimbabwe Mining Development Corp.; and Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Co., among others. The individual named is Thamer Bin Saeed Ahmed al-Shanfari. The Treasury Department said he is an Omani national who has close ties to Mugabe and his top officials and uses his company, Oryx Natural Resources, to "enable Mugabe ... to maintain access to, and derive personal benefit from, various mining ventures in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Under the sanctions, any assets tied to al-Shanfari or to the designated companies that are within U.S. jurisdictions must be frozen, and people living in the United States are prohibited from doing business with them. On Monday, Mugabe and Tsvangirai signed an agreement that paves the way for power-sharing talks to take place in the next few weeks. They will be mediated by South African President Thabo Mbeki, as a representative of the Southern African Development Community, and Jean Ping, chairman of the African Union Commission. Bush said Friday the United States is ready to provide a "substantial assistance package, development aid and normalization with international financial institutions" should those talks result in a new government "that reflects the will of the Zimbabwean people." In the meantime, the president said he is authorizing the use of up to $2.5 million from the U.S. Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund to assist Zimbabwean refugees and those displaced by the violence. In addition, he said the United States will continue efforts to provide food and medical care to Zimbabweans.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Bush signed an executive order on Friday expanding U.S. sanctions against Zimbabwe, the White House announced. Approximately 200 victims of election-related violence have sought refuge outside the U.S. Embassy in Harare, Zimbabwe, this month. "The new executive order significantly enhances our ability to designate individuals and entities connected to the Mugabe regime," Bush stated in a written declaration that characterized the Zimbabwean government under President Robert Mugabe as "illegitimate."

Shortly following the announcement, the Treasury Department revealed that it had designated 17 entities for sanctions—including three government-owned or -controlled companies allegedly employed by Mugabe and his administration "to illegally siphon revenue and foreign exchange from the Zimbabwean people"—along with one individual.

"This action is a direct response to the Mugabe regime's continued politically motivated violence, in defiance of calls from the Southern African Development Community, the African Union, and the United Nations to halt the attacks," the White House said. "The regime has also persisted in its ban on NGO activities that would provide assistance to Zimbabwe's suffering and vulnerable population. No regime should be permitted to disregard the will of its own people and the calls of the international community without facing consequences."

The United States has been advocating for sanctions against Zimbabwe since Mugabe disregarded a U.N. Security Council appeal to postpone the presidential runoff election held on June 27. The vote was originally intended as a runoff between Mugabe and opposition candidate Morgan Tsvangirai, who, according to official government tallies, did not secure an outright victory in the general election. However, Tsvangirai—representing the Movement for Democratic Change—withdrew just before the vote, alleging that Mugabe's supporters had orchestrated a campaign of beatings, intimidation, and murder against his backers.

Earlier this month, Russia and China vetoed a Security Council resolution—championed by the United States, Britain, and France—that would have imposed international sanctions on Mugabe and senior members of his government. Bush expressed his "displeasure" over the vetoes last week, noting that the Treasury and State Departments were simultaneously developing potential unilateral U.S. measures.

Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Jendayi Frazer informed members of Congress last week that more than 100 people have been killed, over 3,000 injured through beatings or torture, and more than 30,000 displaced from their homes as a result of the violence that erupted following the general election.

Among the entities designated by the Treasury Department are the Minerals Marketing Corporation of Zimbabwe—the sole marketing and export agent for all minerals mined in the country except gold and silver—the Zimbabwe Mining Development Corporation, and the Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Company, among others.

The individual named in the sanctions is Thamer Bin Saeed Ahmed al-Shanfari, an Omani national whom the Treasury Department describes as maintaining close ties to Mugabe and his senior officials. According to the department, al-Shanfari uses his company, Oryx Natural Resources, to "enable Mugabe... to maintain access to, and derive personal benefit from, various mining ventures in the Democratic Republic of the Congo." Under the sanctions, any assets belonging to al-Shanfari or the designated companies within U.S. jurisdiction must be frozen, and individuals residing in the United States are prohibited from conducting business with them.

On Monday, Mugabe and Tsvangirai signed an agreement paving the way for power-sharing negotiations to commence in the coming weeks. These talks will be mediated by South African President Thabo Mbeki, representing the Southern African Development Community, and Jean Ping, chairman of the African Union Commission.

Bush indicated on Friday that the United States stands ready to provide a "substantial assistance package, development aid, and normalization with international financial institutions" should these negotiations yield a new government "that reflects the will of the Zimbabwean people."

In the interim, the president announced that he is authorizing the allocation of up to $2.5 million from the U.S. Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund to support Zimbabwean refugees and those displaced by the violence. He further stated that the United States will continue its efforts to provide food and medical care to the people of Zimbabwe.

# U.S. Tightens the Screws on Zimbabwe's Government

The White House announced Friday that President Bush had put his signature on an executive order broadening American sanctions targeting Zimbabwe. This month, roughly 200 people who fell victim to election-related violence have taken refuge just outside the U.S. Embassy grounds in Harare.

In a written statement branding Robert Mugabe's administration "illegitimate," Bush explained that the order "significantly enhances our ability to designate individuals in and entities connected to the Mugabe regime." Shortly after this announcement came out, the Treasury Department revealed it had placed sanctions on 17 entities—among them three state-owned or state-controlled companies that Mugabe's government allegedly used "to illegally siphon revenue and foreign exchange from the Zimbabwean people"—along with a single individual.

According to the White House, this move came in direct response to "the Mugabe regime's continued politically motivated violence," which has persisted despite pleas from the Southern African Development Community, the African Union, and the United Nations to stop the attacks. The statement added that the regime had also kept its prohibition on NGO operations that could otherwise aid Zimbabwe's suffering and vulnerable population, concluding: "No regime should ignore the will of its own people and calls from the international community without consequences."

Washington has been advocating for sanctions against Zimbabwe ever since Mugabe disregarded a U.N. Security Council request to delay the June 27 presidential runoff. That vote was originally meant to pit Mugabe against opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai, who—according to official government results—fell short of an outright victory in the general election. However, Tsvangirai, representing the Movement for Democratic Change, pulled out of the race just before voting began, claiming that Mugabe loyalists had launched a coordinated campaign of violence, intimidation, and killings targeting his supporters.

Earlier in the month, a Security Council resolution backed by the U.S., Britain, and France—which would have slapped international sanctions on Mugabe and his senior officials—was blocked by vetoes from Russia and China. Bush indicated last week that he was "displeased" with this outcome, though he noted that the Treasury and State Departments were already exploring possible unilateral American measures.

Jendayi Frazer, Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs, informed Congress last week that the post-election violence has resulted in over 100 deaths, more than 3,000 injuries from beatings or torture, and over 30,000 people forced from their homes.

Among the companies now under Treasury sanctions are the Minerals Marketing Corp. of Zimbabwe—which handles the exclusive marketing and export of nearly all minerals mined in the country, excluding gold and silver—as well as the Zimbabwe Mining Development Corp. and Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Co., among others. The lone individual targeted, Thamer Bin Saeed Ahmed al-Shanfari, is described by Treasury officials as an Omani national maintaining close relationships with Mugabe and his inner circle. Officials say he uses his firm, Oryx Natural Resources, to help "Mugabe ... maintain access to, and derive personal benefit from, various mining ventures in the Democratic Republic of the Congo."

The sanctions require that any U.S.-based assets belonging to al-Shanfari or the named companies be frozen, while also barring American residents from engaging in business dealings with them.

On Monday, a separate development unfolded when Mugabe and Tsvangirai put their signatures on an agreement setting the stage for power-sharing negotiations in the coming weeks. South African President Thabo Mbeki, representing the Southern African Development Community, along with African Union Commission chairman Jean Ping, will serve as mediators for these talks.

Bush stated Friday that should these negotiations produce a new government "that reflects the will of the Zimbabwean people," the United States stands ready to offer "a substantial assistance package, development aid and normalization with international financial institutions." In the interim, he authorized up to $2.5 million from the U.S. Emergency Refugee and Migration Assistance Fund to support Zimbabwean refugees and those displaced by ongoing violence. The president also pledged that the U.S. would continue working to deliver food and medical assistance to Zimbabwe's population.

# Bush Expands Sanctions Against Mugabe's "Illegitimate" Regime

President Bush signed an executive order on Friday significantly expanding United States sanctions against Zimbabwe, taking the unusual step of formally labeling President Robert Mugabe's government "illegitimate." The move represents a marked escalation in Washington's efforts to isolate the regime amid mounting international concern over political violence and electoral manipulation in the southern African nation.

As part of the expanded sanctions regime, the U.S. Treasury Department designated 17 entities for punitive measures, including three companies that are either owned or controlled by the Zimbabwean government. Additionally, one individual was named in the sanctions. According to Treasury officials, these entities and the individual were targeted for their roles in siphoning revenue away from ordinary Zimbabweans, effectively diverting national resources for the benefit of the ruling elite rather than the population at large.

The White House characterized the sanctions as a direct and necessary response to the Mugabe government's continued campaign of politically motivated violence. Officials emphasized that the regime had repeatedly ignored appeals from key international bodies—including the Southern African Development Community (SADC), the African Union, and the United Nations—all of which had called for an immediate halt to the violence gripping the country. The administration framed the sanctions as a signal that the international community's patience with Mugabe's government had been exhausted.

This latest push for sanctions came in the wake of Mugabe's controversial decision to proceed with a presidential runoff election on June 27, despite an explicit appeal from the U.N. Security Council urging postponement of the vote. The election had already been thrown into turmoil after opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai withdrew his candidacy, citing an escalating campaign of violence and intimidation directed at his supporters. Tsvangirai's withdrawal effectively stripped the runoff of any genuine democratic contest, further reinforcing international perceptions that the vote would lack legitimacy.

The diplomatic tensions surrounding Zimbabwe had already been on display earlier in the month, when Russia and China exercised their veto power at the U.N. Security Council to block a resolution on the crisis. That resolution, which had been championed by the United States, Britain, and France, sought stronger international action against the Mugabe government. Its defeat highlighted the deep divisions among permanent Security Council members over how to address the deteriorating situation in Zimbabwe, leaving Washington and its allies to pursue unilateral and multilateral sanctions as an alternative avenue for pressuring Mugabe's regime.

**Bush Signs Executive Order Expanding Sanctions Against Zimbabwe's Mugabe**

*Washington (CNN)* — President Bush signed an executive order Friday expanding U.S. sanctions against Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe and members of his government, citing continued human rights abuses and the erosion of democratic processes in the southern African nation.

The order broadens existing sanctions first imposed in 2003, adding new individuals and entities to a list of those subject to asset freezes and travel bans. Administration officials said the move was a direct response to violence and intimidation surrounding Zimbabwe's electoral process, as well as the government's crackdown on political opposition figures.

"The situation in Zimbabwe continues to deteriorate under President Mugabe's leadership," Bush said in a statement released by the White House. "This regime has shown a blatant disregard for the will of the Zimbabwean people and has used violence, intimidation and fraud to cling to power."

The expanded sanctions target additional government officials, military and security officers, and business figures with close ties to Mugabe's ZANU-PF party. Treasury Department officials said the goal is to increase pressure on the inner circle sustaining Mugabe's rule while limiting the impact on ordinary Zimbabweans, who have suffered under hyperinflation and severe food shortages.

"We are targeting those responsible for the violence and repression, not the people of Zimbabwe," a senior Treasury official said on background. "The Zimbabwean people have suffered enough."

The order comes amid mounting international criticism of Mugabe's government following a disputed presidential runoff election that observers, including the United Nations and African Union, said was marred by violence against opposition supporters. Opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai withdrew from the runoff, citing attacks on his supporters, leaving Mugabe to claim victory in a vote widely condemned as illegitimate.

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice called on regional leaders, particularly South Africa, to take a firmer stance against Mugabe. "Quiet diplomacy has not worked," Rice said. "It is time for the region to speak with one voice and make clear that the results of a sham election will not be recognized."

The White House said it would continue to work with international partners, including the United Nations Security Council, to increase pressure on Mugabe's government. However, previous attempts to pass a U.N. resolution imposing broader international sanctions have stalled amid opposition from Russia and China, both of which hold veto power on the Security Council.

Zimbabwe's government dismissed the new sanctions as an example of Western interference. A spokesman for Mugabe's administration accused Washington of pursuing a "regime change agenda" and said the sanctions would only worsen conditions for ordinary citizens.

Human rights groups largely welcomed the move but cautioned that targeted sanctions alone were unlikely to force Mugabe from power. "This sends an important signal, but it's not a silver bullet," said one analyst with a Washington-based human rights organization. "Real change will require sustained regional pressure, particularly from South Africa."

Zimbabwe's economy has collapsed in recent years, with inflation estimated in the millions of percent and unemployment above 80%. Millions of Zimbabweans have fled to neighboring countries, particularly South Africa, in search of work and stability.

The White House said additional sanctions could follow if the situation in Zimbabwe does not improve.

CNN's State Department and White House correspondents contributed to this report.

# NEWS WIRE REPORT

**FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**

## Bush Administration Escalates Pressure on Mugabe Regime Amid Zimbabwe Crisis

WASHINGTON — The Bush administration intensified its campaign against Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe's government this week, combining fresh Treasury Department sanctions with diplomatic pressure at the United Nations, even as a power-sharing agreement between Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai showed signs of strain.

**Treasury Sanctions**

The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities linked to the Mugabe government, freezing assets and barring financial transactions with U.S. persons. Officials said the move was intended to tighten the economic noose around figures deemed responsible for human rights abuses, electoral fraud, and the broader collapse of governance in Zimbabwe. The designations expanded an existing sanctions framework first imposed under Executive Order 13288 in 2003 and subsequently broadened in later years.

A senior Treasury official said the sanctions were "aimed squarely at those who have enriched themselves while the Zimbabwean people suffer," citing hyperinflation, food shortages, and political violence that have marked Mugabe's nearly three-decade rule.

**UN Security Council Veto**

At the United Nations, the administration pressed for a Security Council resolution that would have imposed international sanctions and an arms embargo on Zimbabwe, citing the flawed 2008 elections and subsequent violence against opposition supporters. However, the measure was blocked by vetoes from Russia and China, both permanent Security Council members, who argued that Zimbabwe's crisis did not constitute a threat to international peace and security and objected to what they characterized as interference in the country's internal affairs.

U.S. Ambassador to the UN Zalmay Khalilzad expressed sharp disappointment, telling reporters the veto sent "the wrong signal" to Mugabe's government and undermined efforts to hold Harare accountable. Washington vowed to continue pursuing unilateral and multilateral pressure despite the setback at the Council.

**Power-Sharing Deal Under Scrutiny**

The renewed U.S. pressure comes as Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai attempt to implement a power-sharing agreement, brokered with regional mediation, under which Tsvangirai would assume the role of prime minister while Mugabe retains the presidency. The deal, signed after months of political violence and a widely disputed run-off election that Tsvangirai withdrew from, has been hailed by some African leaders as a path toward stability.

The Bush administration, however, has voiced skepticism, with officials cautioning that the agreement must be judged by implementation rather than signatures. "We will be watching closely to see whether this arrangement produces real change on the ground — an end to violence, restoration of the rule of law, and genuine power-sharing — rather than simply providing cover for the further consolidation of Mugabe's authority," a State Department spokesperson said.

Analysts note that Washington's continued sanctions regime signals its intent to maintain pressure on Mugabe loyalists even as the political settlement unfolds, reflecting broader concerns that the deal could leave Mugabe's inner circle largely insulated from accountability.

**Broader Context**

The developments underscore the Bush administration's dual-track approach to Zimbabwe in its final months in office: pursuing punitive financial measures against the Mugabe government while working — with limited success — to build international consensus for a coordinated response through the UN. With the Security Council effort stalled, U.S. officials indicated further unilateral designations targeting Mugabe allies remain under consideration.

*—END—*

# U.S. Tightens Pressure on Zimbabwe Amid Election Violence Crisis

**WASHINGTON** — The United States government has escalated its criticism of Zimbabwe's political leadership and moved to strengthen punitive measures against President Robert Mugabe's regime, citing continued violence and intimidation surrounding the country's disputed electoral process.

## Background on the Crisis

Zimbabwe's political turmoil stems from a presidential election that international observers have widely characterized as neither free nor fair. The initial round of voting failed to produce a decisive winner, forcing a runoff between Mugabe, who has ruled Zimbabwe since independence in 1980, and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai of the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC).

In the weeks following the first round, human rights organizations and Western governments documented widespread reports of violence, including attacks on opposition supporters, displacement of rural populations believed to support the MDC, and intimidation campaigns allegedly orchestrated by state security forces and ruling ZANU-PF party militias. The violence ultimately prompted Tsvangirai to withdraw from the runoff election, stating that conditions made a legitimate vote impossible, though Mugabe proceeded with the poll regardless.

## U.S. Response

American officials condemned the runoff as illegitimate and called for a political settlement that reflects the will of the Zimbabwean people as expressed in the initial round of voting.

"The results of a sham election that was neither free nor fair should not be used to legitimize an illegitimate outcome," said a senior State Department official, echoing language used throughout the administration's public statements on the crisis.

The White House pressed for expanded international sanctions, including targeted measures against Zimbabwean officials tied to the violence, and pushed for United Nations Security Council action—though such efforts faced resistance from Security Council members with reservations about intervention.

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice indicated that Washington would work closely with regional partners, including South Africa and the Southern African Development Community (SADC), to press for a negotiated transition, while cautioning that any agreement must genuinely reflect the democratic aspirations of Zimbabweans rather than simply preserve Mugabe's grip on power.

## Sanctions and Diplomatic Measures

The U.S. Treasury Department moved to expand its sanctions list, freezing assets and imposing travel bans on additional individuals connected to the Mugabe government, including business figures believed to be financing ruling party operations. Officials emphasized that these measures were designed to target the political elite responsible for the violence rather than the broader Zimbabwean population, which was already suffering under hyperinflation and economic collapse.

## Regional and International Dimension

Washington's response was complicated by divisions within the international community. While the United States, United Kingdom, and other Western nations pushed for a strong condemnation and potential Security Council sanctions, several African nations and China expressed reluctance, favoring continued mediation efforts led by South African President Thabo Mbeki.

Critics of the U.S. approach argued that sanctions alone were insufficient without stronger backing from regional powers, given Zimbabwe's economic dependence on neighboring states.

## Outlook

As of the crisis's peak, U.S. officials continued to advocate for a power-sharing arrangement or transitional government that would include genuine opposition participation, while maintaining that Mugabe's runoff "victory" carried no international legitimacy. The administration signaled that additional sanctions remained under consideration should the political impasse continue without meaningful reform.
